doc.title: Ruth Lion interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

chapter: Alfred Lion and the founding of Blue Note
title: Hammond's 'Spirituals to Swing' concert and the first Blue Note idea
summary: Alfred came to the US around 1937, joined a jazz club, and heard Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons at Carnegie Hall, asking for a twelve-inch record.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Well let’s talk about that. Because he finally came to the U.S. to stay, and that was what year? About what year? After Chile.

I think that might have been about 1937. And he wanted to get more immersed, enmeshed in jazz. And he joined a club in New Jersey. He lived in New York. He joined a club in New Jersey. I don’t know exactly what they called it, but it was a jazz — like people who just loved the music. And they collected the records and they played the records, and I mean they’d just go wild over what they were hearing. And so John Hammond gave a concert, and I do — someone sent me from Japan a copy of that concert, which — I’ve been too appreciative of it to even play it — but this is the concert that Alfred began Blue Note records with. Because he used to see John Hammond — Alfred was always working, working, working — and he’d see him in the post office.

And Hammond thought well gee this guy’s a little bit, what is it, you know, I mean he never stopped working. Alfred could do five things at the same time. And know what he was doing. So he met, he would see him in the post office, and so he said, “You know I’d like you to come and hear my concert at Carnegie Hall, ‘Spirituals to Swing.’ And Alfred said, “Oh I’d love to.” And of course he went and there he happened to hear these two guys.
Sure, they did the piano duets there.

Yeah. Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons. And so he went backstage. I can get a little bit of the feeling that he must have had. I mean because when you hear this record, even though today we might consider it dated but it had such a vitality to it. And Alfred being a person who reacted immediately to something that he really liked, he went backstage and he said, “I belong to a club of people who love jazz. Would you make a twelve-inch record so you wouldn’t have to stop playing? You could just play and play and play.” Because they only had, I think at that time, I don’t know I really am not able to — I’m too excited to tell you, — but you could only play for maybe three minutes. And so he said, “You please come and play and you don’t have to stop.” So the guys said, “Well will you pay us?” And he said, “Well what will you charge?” They said, “A hundred dollars.” So Alfred said, “Yes, I’ll pay you.” And he did. And he made the records, and he played them for his friends, and his friends all wanted copies, and more people wanted copies, and before he knew it, he was in Blue Note records. So that was John Hammond, whom I had the pleasure of talking with and really telling how much I appreciated his making that life possible. I don’t think Alfred would have gotten into business had it not been for that.
